subject: Computer Networking
title: DNS Security
description: A quick, practical guide to DNS Security.

hook.text: DNS is the phone book of the internet. Poison the phone book and you can redirect anyone anywhere.

buildup.text: DNS cache poisoning injects fake records into a resolver. Users get sent to malicious sites without knowing.

discovery.text: DNSSEC adds cryptographic signatures to DNS records. Resolvers can verify answers haven't been tampered with.

twist.text: DNS queries also leak your browsing habits. DNS-over-HTTPS encrypts them so only the resolver sees your lookups.

climax.text: Security-focused DNS providers like 1.1.1.1 and 9.9.9.9 block known malicious domains automatically.

punchline.text: Secure DNS means trustworthy answers and private questions.

quiz.question: What does DNSSEC protect against?
options: Tampered DNS records and cache poisoning

details.summary: DNS security protects the domain name system from attacks like cache poisoning, hijacking, and tunneling. DNSSEC validates response authenticity with cryptographic signatures. DNS filtering blocks access to known malicious domains.
details.whyItMatters: DNS is a critical attack vector because compromising it redirects users invisibly. DNS security prevents attackers from manipulating name resolution to intercept traffic or redirect users to malicious sites.
takeaways: DNSSEC validates DNS responses with cryptographic signatures
DNS filtering blocks connections to known malicious domains
DNS tunneling can exfiltrate data through seemingly normal queries

faq.question: What is DNS cache poisoning?
faq.answer: An attacker injects forged DNS records into a resolver's cache, redirecting users to malicious IP addresses. When users request a legitimate domain, they get the poisoned answer and connect to the attacker's server. DNSSEC prevents this by cryptographically signing DNS records.

faq.question: How does DNS tunneling work?
faq.answer: Attackers encode data in DNS query names and responses, creating a covert communication channel. Since DNS traffic is rarely blocked, this technique bypasses firewalls. Monitoring for unusually long domain names, high query volumes, and abnormal record types helps detect DNS tunneling.
